abstract: Perceptually, one of the strongest memory colors is skin tone. Get it wrong and it is hard to miss. Image adjustments are commonly applied for preference-based image enhancement. Because these adjustments are performed across a variety of color spaces, it is important to understand their effects on skin tone appearance. In this article, results of a psychovisual experiment that explores the perception of skin tone under changes in hue, chroma, and intensity are presented. By combining the effects each axis has on the perception of different skin tones, viewer expectations of color appearance can be evaluated. The experimental results convey a low tolerance for changes in hue when altering intensity and chroma and a high tolerance for changes in intensity across all adjustments. When altering intensity, the results present changes in chroma that follow the shape of the ITU-R BT.2124 (ITP) gamut hull. There was some variability between skin tones. This speaks to how individual skin tone classification may be helpful to preserve appearance following adjustment.

authors.bio: Jake Zuena is an applied vision science engineer at Dolby Laborato?ries, Sunnyvale, CA. In this role, he develops and improves core Dolby imaging technology as well as performs research to model human perception for the design of image-processing algorithms. In 2018, he completed an internship at Warner Bros. Studios, Burbank, CA, in the Emerging Technology Division, focusing on color and imaging science. He received a BS degree in motion picture science from the Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT), Rochester, NY, in 2019. While at RIT, he performed a senior research project to assess the creative preference of highly saturated colors in content mastered for wide color gamut display.
authors.name: Jake Zuena

authors.bio: Jaclyn Pytlarz is a senior staff researcher at Dolby Laboratories, Sunnyvale, CA, where she leads Dolby’s Vision Science Research Organization. Her research includes studying human perception surrounding color mapping, accessibility, and display management algorithms for high dynamic range and wide color gamut imagery. She holds a BS degree in motion picture science from the Rochester Institute of Technology, Rochester, NY, and an MS degree in computational and mathematical engineering from Stanford University, Stanford, CA. Prior to joining Dolby, she worked as an intern for both the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, Los Angeles, CA, and iCONN Video Production, Mount Vernon, OH. She has been awarded the IET Best Young Professional Award and the TVNewsCheck Technology Woman to Watch Award and has been elevated to SMPTE Fellow.
authors.name: Jaclyn Pytlarz
